claim: The B cell antigen receptor (BCR) is a 1:1 complex between the membrane-bound immunoglobulin (mIg) molecule and the Igα/Igβ-heterodimer in its monomeric form.
source: In its monomeric form, the BCR is a 1:1 complex between the membrane-bound immunoglobulin (mIg) molecule and the Igα/Igβ-heterodimer (Schamel and Reth, 2000; Tolar et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Schamel and Reth, 2000; Tolar et al., 2005).

claim: The cytoplasmic tails of both Igα and Igβ carry an immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif (ITAM).
source: The cytoplasmic tails of both Igα and Igβ carry an immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif (ITAM), the tyrosines of which are phosphorylated by Src family protein tyrosine kinases such as Lyn and the spleen tyrosine kinase (Syk) (Schmitz et al., 1996; Pao et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Schmitz et al., 1996; Pao et al., 1998).

claim: ITAM tyrosines are phosphorylated by Src family protein tyrosine kinases such as Lyn and Syk.
source: The cytoplasmic tails of both Igα and Igβ carry an immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif (ITAM), the tyrosines of which are phosphorylated by Src family protein tyrosine kinases such as Lyn and the spleen tyrosine kinase (Syk) (Schmitz et al., 1996; Pao et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Schmitz et al., 1996; Pao et al., 1998).

claim: Lyn predominantly phosphorylates only the first ITAM tyrosine.
source: In contrast to Lyn, which predominantly phosphorylates only the first ITAM tyrosine, Syk phosphorylates both tyrosines and subsequently binds the double-phosphorylated ITAM (ppITAM) via its tandem SH2 domains (Futterer et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Futterer et al., 1998).

claim: Syk phosphorylates both ITAM tyrosines and subsequently binds the double-phosphorylated ITAM (ppITAM) via its tandem SH2 domains.
source: In contrast to Lyn, which predominantly phosphorylates only the first ITAM tyrosine, Syk phosphorylates both tyrosines and subsequently binds the double-phosphorylated ITAM (ppITAM) via its tandem SH2 domains (Futterer et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Futterer et al., 1998).

claim: The binding of Syk to a ppITAM sequence results in the rapid phosphorylation of ITAM tyrosines of neighboring receptors.
source: The binding of Syk to a ppITAM sequence results in the rapid phosphorylation of ITAM tyrosines of neighboring receptors. The resulting increased Syk recruitment generates a positive feedback that amplifies signal transduction from the BCR (Rolli et al., 2002; Mukherjee et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Rolli et al., 2002; Mukherjee et al., 2013).

claim: Increased Syk recruitment generates a positive feedback that amplifies signal transduction from the BCR.
source: The binding of Syk to a ppITAM sequence results in the rapid phosphorylation of ITAM tyrosines of neighboring receptors. The resulting increased Syk recruitment generates a positive feedback that amplifies signal transduction from the BCR (Rolli et al., 2002; Mukherjee et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Rolli et al., 2002; Mukherjee et al., 2013).

claim: Syk interacts only with the activated but not with the resting BCR.
source: A PLA study showed that Syk interacts only with the activated but not with the resting BCR (Infantino et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Infantino et al., 2010).

claim: B cells can be activated by exposure to the F-actin inhibitor Latrunculin A (Lat-A).
source: Indeed, B cells can be activated not only by exposure to antigen but also to the F-actin inhibitor Latrunculin A (Lat-A), suggesting that the actin cytoskeleton protects the resting BCR (Treanor et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Treanor et al., 2010).

claim: The actin cytoskeleton protects the resting BCR.
source: Indeed, B cells can be activated not only by exposure to antigen but also to the F-actin inhibitor Latrunculin A (Lat-A), suggesting that the actin cytoskeleton protects the resting BCR (Treanor et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Treanor et al., 2010) and the inference that Lat-A activation suggests cytoskeletal protection.

claim: The cytoskeleton limits the free diffusion of receptors.
source: The cytoskeleton is also limiting the free diffusion of receptors (Kusumi et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Kusumi et al., 2005).

claim: B cell activation is accompanied by cytoskeleton remodeling and increased BCR mobility.
source: In line with this, B cell activation is accompanied by cytoskeleton remodeling and increased BCR mobility.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: BCR mobility is reduced in membrane areas enriched in ezrin-radixin-moesin (ERM) proteins.
source: Furthermore, it has been shown that BCR mobility is reduced in membrane areas enriched in ezrin-radixin-moesin (ERM) proteins (Harwood and Batista, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Harwood and Batista, 2011).

claim: The cytoskeleton is required for microcluster formation and receptor internalization.
source: However, and complicating matters further, the cytoskeleton not only plays an inhibitory, but also an activating role during B cell activation, as it is required for microcluster formation and receptor internalization (Brown and Song, 2001; Cheng et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Brown and Song, 2001; Cheng et al., 2001).

claim: Mature B lymphocytes coexpress an IgM-BCR and an IgD-BCR on their surface.
source: Mature B lymphocytes coexpress an IgM-BCR and an IgD-BCR on their surface, the latter being the dominant receptors on these cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: IgD-BCR is the dominant receptor on mature B lymphocytes.
source: Mature B lymphocytes coexpress an IgM-BCR and an IgD-BCR on their surface, the latter being the dominant receptors on these cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: IgM-BCR and IgD-BCR have distinct signaling functions and diffusion behaviors on the B cell surface.
source: These two receptors have distinct signaling functions and diffusion behaviors on the B cell surface but the molecular basis for these differences is poorly understood (Kim and Reth, 1995; Treanor et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Kim and Reth, 1995; Treanor et al., 2010).

claim: The cross-linking model (CLM) assumes that most of the 100,000 BCR complexes on the surface of a B cell are monomeric.
source: The cross-linking model (CLM) assumes that most of the 100,000 BCR complexes on the surface of a B cell are monomeric and that cross-linking of two BCR monomers by a polyvalent antigen initiates the signaling process (Metzger, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Metzger, 1992).

claim: According to the cross-linking model, cross-linking of two BCR monomers by a polyvalent antigen initiates the signaling process.
source: The cross-linking model (CLM) assumes that most of the 100,000 BCR complexes on the surface of a B cell are monomeric and that cross-linking of two BCR monomers by a polyvalent antigen initiates the signaling process (Metzger, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Metzger, 1992).

claim: The conformation-induced oligomerization model (CIOM) proposes that antigen binding induces a conformational change of the monomeric BCR, resulting in the dimerization of the membrane proximal CH domain of the BCR followed by receptor signaling.
source: Similarly, the conformation-induced oligomerization model (CIOM) proposes that antigen binding induces a conformational change of the monomeric BCR, resulting in the dimerization of the membrane proximal CH domain of the BCR followed by receptor signaling (Tolar and Pierce, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Tolar and Pierce, 2010).

claim: Antigen receptors on resting T and B cells are organized in nanoclusters inside protein islands.
source: However, recent studies show that antigen receptors on resting T and B cells are not uniformly distributed but are rather organized in nanoclusters inside protein islands (Lillemeier et al., 2006, 2010; Mattila et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Lillemeier et al., 2006, 2010; Mattila et al., 2013).

claim: The resting BCR forms stable dimers on the cell surface.
source: Furthermore, with a quantitative bifluorescence complementation (BiFC) assay, we found that the resting BCR forms stable dimers on the cell surface while a BCR mutant that cannot form dimers is hyperactive and cannot be stably expressed on the B cell surface (Yang and Reth, 2010b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Yang and Reth, 2010b).

claim: A BCR mutant that cannot form dimers is hyperactive and cannot be stably expressed on the B cell surface.
source: Furthermore, with a quantitative bifluorescence complementation (BiFC) assay, we found that the resting BCR forms stable dimers on the cell surface while a BCR mutant that cannot form dimers is hyperactive and cannot be stably expressed on the B cell surface (Yang and Reth, 2010b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Yang and Reth, 2010b).

claim: The dissociation-activation model (DAM) proposes that BCR activation is initiated by the dissociation of signaling-inert BCR oligomers.
source: We thus have proposed the dissociation-activation model (DAM) whereby BCR activation is initiated by the dissociation of signaling-inert BCR oligomers (Yang and Reth, 2010a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Yang and Reth, 2010a).

claim: Fab-PLA has a detection range of 10-20 nm.
source: By coupling the DNA oligos directly to primary antibodies (1-PLA), or to Fab fragments (Fab-PLA), we narrowed the detection range of this assay down to 10–40 nm and 10–20 nm, respectively (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of the method in the text.

claim: 1-PLA has a detection range of 10-40 nm.
source: By coupling the DNA oligos directly to primary antibodies (1-PLA), or to Fab fragments (Fab-PLA), we narrowed the detection range of this assay down to 10–40 nm and 10–20 nm, respectively (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of the method in the text.

claim: 2-PLA has a detection range of 10-80 nm.
source: The classical PLA method (2-PLA) involves secondary antibodies and detects the proximity of two molecules in the 10–80 nm range.
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of the method in the text.

claim: Only Fab-PLA showed a clear difference in the relative IgM:IgM conformation or distance between resting and activated B cells.
source: However, only the Fab-PLA showed a clear difference in the relative IgM:IgM conformation or distance between resting and activated B cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F comparing the three PLA methods.

claim: The Fab-PLA differences between resting and activated B cells are statistically significant.
source: The PLA data were quantified by the BlobFinder software (Allalou and Wahlby, 2009) and showed that the Fab-PLA differences between resting and activated B cells are statistically significant (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantified data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Upon B cell activation, mIgM molecules move further than 20 nm apart from each other so that their proximity can be still detected by 1-PLA but no longer by Fab-PLA.
source: The IgM–IgM PLA studies suggests that, upon B cell activation, mIgM molecules move further than 20 nm apart from each other so that their proximity can be still detected by 1-PLA but no longer by Fab-PLA (Figure 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the PLA data and illustrated in Figure 1J.

claim: Fab-PLA detects pentameric IgM but not loosely spaced monomeric IgM on NIP-coupled latex beads.
source: The FACScan analysis of these beads shows that Fab-PLA detects the pentameric IgM but not the loosely spaced monomeric IgM whereas 1-PLA detects both forms of IgM equally well (Figure 2C, compare upper and lower panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C comparing Fab-PLA and 1-PLA detection of monomeric and pentameric IgM on beads.

claim: 1-PLA detects both monomeric and pentameric IgM equally well on NIP-coupled latex beads.
source: The FACScan analysis of these beads shows that Fab-PLA detects the pentameric IgM but not the loosely spaced monomeric IgM whereas 1-PLA detects both forms of IgM equally well (Figure 2C, compare upper and lower panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C comparing Fab-PLA and 1-PLA detection of monomeric and pentameric IgM on beads.

claim: The constant domains of pentameric IgM are no further apart from each other than 5-6 nm.
source: In a recent structural study of pentameric IgM, it was shown that the constant domains of IgM are no further apart from each other than 5–6 nm (Czajkowsky and Shao, 2009), a distance that can be easily bridged by the anti-IgM Fabs used for the Fab-PLA method.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Czajkowsky and Shao, 2009).

claim: The IgD:IgD Fab-PLA detects the wild-type receptor but barely detects a mutant IgD-BCR that is defective in oligomer formation.
source: In case of the IgD-BCR, we found direct evidence for this notion, because the IgD:IgD Fab-PLA detects the wild-type receptor but barely detects a mutant IgD-BCR that is defective in oligomer formation (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3 comparing wild-type and mutant IgD-BCR.

claim: B cell activation is accompanied by the opening of tightly packed BCR oligomers.
source: Together, these studies suggest that B cell activation is accompanied by the opening of tightly packed BCR oligomers as predicted by the DAM hypothesis (Yang and Reth, 2010a, 2010b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the PLA data presented in the manuscript and citations to previous work (Yang and Reth, 2010a, 2010b).

claim: The IgM:IgM and IgD:IgD Fab-PLA signal is lost upon exposure of B cells to antigen.
source: The quantification of the Fab-PLA analysis of B1-8 (Figure 4A, right panel) and TKO-MD (Figure 4B) B cells shows that in each case, the IgM:IgM and IgD:IgD Fab-PLA signal is lost upon exposure of B cells to antigen.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: The Fab-PLA signal is lost when B1-8 B cells are stimulated with pervanadate and Lat-A.
source: The Fab-PLA signal is also lost when we stimulated B1-8 B cells apart from antigen with BCR-activating drugs such as pervanadate (Perv) and Lat-A (Figure 4C), which alter the phosphorylation/dephosphorylation equilibrium and inhibit actin polymerization, respectively (Secrist et al., 1993; Treanor et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and citations to previous work (Secrist et al., 1993; Treanor et al., 2010).

claim: PP2 treatment only delays the opening of the IgM-BCR oligomer.
source: While the PP2-treatment only delays the opening of the IgM-BCR oligomer, this process no longer occurs in the presence of the Syk inhibitor R406 (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: The Syk inhibitor R406 prevents the opening of the IgM-BCR oligomer.
source: While the PP2-treatment only delays the opening of the IgM-BCR oligomer, this process no longer occurs in the presence of the Syk inhibitor R406 (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: Syk not only signals downstream but also alters the BCR conformation via an inside-out signaling process.
source: The IgM:IgM Fab-PLA results of these genetically altered B cells were similar to those previously observed using kinase inhibitors and suggests that Syk not only signals downstream but also alters the BCR conformation via an inside-out signaling process.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Lyn- or Syk-deficient B cells (Figure 5C) and inference from the results.

claim: The BCR/Syk interaction is induced within 1 min of Lat-A treatment.
source: This analysis shows that the BCR/Syk interaction is induced within 1 min of Lat-A treatment (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: PP2 delays the BCR/Syk interaction.
source: This interaction is delayed by PP2 whereas the Syk inhibitor R406 completely blocks the recruitment of Syk to the BCR.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the Igα:Syk Fab-PLA experiments.

claim: The Syk inhibitor R406 completely blocks the recruitment of Syk to the BCR.
source: This interaction is delayed by PP2 whereas the Syk inhibitor R406 completely blocks the recruitment of Syk to the BCR.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the Igα:Syk Fab-PLA experiments.

claim: The Syk/BCR inside-out signaling process increases the sensitivity of B cells to low doses of antigen.
source: This titration experiment supports the notion that the Syk/BCR inside-out signaling increases the sensitivity of B cells to low doses of antigen.
evidence: This claim is supported by the antigen titration experiment shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Syk-sufficient cells require 10 ng/ml of antigen to lose the IgM:IgM Fab-PLA signal.
source: Syk-sufficient cells require 10 ng/ml of antigen to lose the IgM:IgM Fab-PLA signal whereas B cell exposed for 60 min to the Syk inhibitor lose the IgM:IgM Fab-PLA signal only at 10–50 times higher (250–500 ng/ml) antigen doses.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the antigen titration experiment shown in Figure 5G.

claim: B cells exposed for 60 min to the Syk inhibitor lose the IgM:IgM Fab-PLA signal only at 10-50 times higher (250-500 ng/ml) antigen doses.
source: Syk-sufficient cells require 10 ng/ml of antigen to lose the IgM:IgM Fab-PLA signal whereas B cell exposed for 60 min to the Syk inhibitor lose the IgM:IgM Fab-PLA signal only at 10–50 times higher (250–500 ng/ml) antigen doses.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the antigen titration experiment shown in Figure 5G.

claim: S2 cells co-expressing the IgM-BCR together with a GFP-Syk fusion protein show drastically reduced IgM:IgM Fab-PLA signal.
source: The IgM:IgM Fab-PLA signal is drastically reduced on S2 cells co-expressing the IgM-BCR together with a GFP-Syk fusion protein (Figure 6A, second panel and Figure 6B, second bar).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: S2 cells expressing the IgM-BCR only together with nLyn-Syk-KD show tyrosine phosphorylation of Igα but no loss of the IgM:IgM Fab-PLA signal.
source: S2 cells expressing the IgM-BCR only together with nLyn-Syk-KD show tyrosine phosphorylation of Igα (data not shown) but no loss of the IgM:IgM Fab-PLA signal (Figure 6A, third panel and Figure 6B, third bar).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: It is the binding of Syk to the receptor, not the phosphorylation of the ITAM tyrosines, that results in the opening of BCR oligomers.
source: Together these data indicate that it is not the phosphorylation of the ITAM tyrosines but rather the binding of the Syk to the receptor that results in the opening of BCR oligomers (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the S2 cell experiments shown in Figures 6A and 6B, and inference from the results.

claim: CD19 is found in close association with the activated but not with the resting IgM-BCR.
source: This analysis shows that CD19 is only found in close association with the activated but not with the resting IgM-BCR (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: CD19 is found together with the resting IgD-BCR and dissociates from this receptor upon BCR activation.
source: Interestingly, in this assay, the results for the IgD-BCR were opposite to those observed for IgM. CD19 is found together with the resting IgD-BCR and dissociates from this receptor upon BCR activation (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The CD19:BCR interaction is Ig class specific and remodeled upon B cell activation.
source: The quantification of these data shows, for the first time, that the CD19:BCR interaction is Ig class specific and remodeled upon B cell activation (Figure 7A,B, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: CD20 displays the same class-specific BCR interaction as CD19.
source: By IgM:CD20 and IgD:CD20 Fab-PLA, we found that CD20 displays the same class-specific BCR interaction as CD19 (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: On resting B cells, GM1 gangliosides are found in close proximity to the IgD-BCR.
source: The IgD:CTB and IgM:CTB PLA showed that on resting B cells, GM1 gangliosides are found in close proximity to the IgD-BCR, whereas the IgM-BCR gains access to large amounts of these lipids only upon B cell activation (Figure 7H,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 7G and 7H.

claim: The IgM-BCR gains access to large amounts of GM1 gangliosides only upon B cell activation.
source: The IgD:CTB and IgM:CTB PLA showed that on resting B cells, GM1 gangliosides are found in close proximity to the IgD-BCR, whereas the IgM-BCR gains access to large amounts of these lipids only upon B cell activation (Figure 7H,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 7G and 7H.

claim: The IgM-BCR and the IgD-BCR are localized on the B cell surface in different membrane areas that are reorganized upon B cell activation.
source: Together, these studies suggest that the IgM-BCR and the IgD-BCR are localized on the B cell surface in different membrane areas that are reorganized upon B cell activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the CD19, CD20, and GM1 ganglioside proximity data and inference from the results.

claim: Antigen-dependent B cell activation is accompanied by a transition from a tightly packed BCR oligomer to a more loosely spaced BCR-antigen or BCR-Syk clusters that can no longer be detected by Fab-PLA.
source: Our analysis suggest that antigen-dependent B cell activation is accompanied by a transition from a tightly packed BCR oligomer to a more loosely spaced BCR-antigen or BCR-Syk clusters that can no longer be detected by Fab-PLA (Figure 1J, Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by the Fab-PLA data and inference from the results, illustrated in Figures 1J and 5H.

claim: The kinase Syk is necessary and sufficient for the opening of the oligomeric BCR.
source: Our findings support the DAM hypothesis (Yang and Reth, 2010a, 2010b), and in addition show for the first time that the kinase Syk is necessary and sufficient for the opening of the oligomeric BCR.
evidence: This claim is supported by the Syk inhibitor and gain-of-function experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Receptor dissociation and aggregation are not mutually exclusive events but rather processes that occur at different size levels and time points during B cell activation.
source: Receptor dissociation and aggregation are thus not mutually exclusive events but rather processes that occur at different size levels and time points during B cell activation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the integration of nanoscale PLA data with previous live cell imaging studies.

claim: Nanoclusters containing opened BCR presumably aggregate to form the microclusters previously detected by live cell imaging studies of activated lymphocytes.
source: Nanoclusters containing opened BCR presumably aggregate to form the microclusters previously detected by live cell imaging studies of activated lymphocytes.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the PLA data and previous imaging studies.

claim: CD19-deficient mice are defective in B cell development and function.
source: Indeed, CD19-deficient mice are defective in B cell development and function (Rickert et al., 1995; Sato et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Rickert et al., 1995; Sato et al., 1997).

claim: CD19 and IgM co-cap on activated B cells.
source: It has been shown that CD19 and IgM co-cap on activated B cells (Pesando et al., 1989) and it thus was no surprise to find the two receptors in close proximity to each other on these cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Pesando et al., 1989).

claim: The resting IgD-BCR is associated with lipid ordered domains.
source: The resting IgD-BCR seems to be also associated with lipid ordered domains, as indicated by the proximity of this receptor to GM1 gangliosides and the GPI-linked protein CD52.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the proximity data for GM1 gangliosides and CD52.

claim: The co-localization of the IgM-BCR with CD19 and lipid ordered domains is a hallmark of B cell activation.
source: The co-localization of the IgM-BCR with CD19 and lipid ordered domains is a hallmark of B cell activation but this is apparently not the case for the IgD-BCR on resting B lymphocytes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the proximity data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The IgD-BCR protein islands likely contain inhibitory factors which prevent signaling.
source: Thus, the IgD-BCR protein islands are likely to contain inhibitory factors which prevent signaling and we are currently searching for such molecules by Fab-PLA.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the observation that IgD-BCR is in lipid ordered domains on resting cells.

claim: An inside-out-signaling mechanism has previously been found to play a role in the activation of CD28 by the TCR.
source: An inside-out-signaling mechanism has previously been found to play a role in the activation of CD28 by the TCR (Sanchez-Lockhart et al., 2011) and the regulation of integrin receptors such as LFA-1 (Wang, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Sanchez-Lockhart et al., 2011; Wang, 2012).

claim: In integrins, the binding of talin to the cytosolic tail of the β-chain displaces the α-tail from its complex with the β-tail, moving the two tails apart.
source: In the latter case it is the binding of talin to the cytosolic tail of the β-chain that displaces the α-tail from its complex with the β-tail, thus moving the two tails apart.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about integrin inside-out signaling.

claim: The intracellular movement of integrin tails is translated into an extracellular conformational change that opens the integrin for ligand binding.
source: This intracellular movement is translated into an extracellular conformational change that opens the integrin for ligand binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about integrin inside-out signaling.

claim: The binding of Syk to the phosphorylated ITAM sequences may distort the Igα/Igβ tails in such a way that it destabilizes the BCR oligomer, resulting in BCR opening and activation.
source: Similarly, the binding of Syk to the phosphorylated ITAM sequences may distort the Igα/Igβ tails in such a way that it destabilizes the BCR oligomer, thus resulting in BCR opening and activation.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on analogy with integrin inside-out signaling.

claim: A mutation of the disulfide bridge between Igα and Igβ, in combination with a transmembrane mutation of mIgD, prevents the formation of the IgD-BCR oligomer.
source: In line with this scenario, we found that a mutation of the disulfide bridge between Igα and Igβ, in combination with a transmembrane mutation of mIgD, prevents the formation of the IgD-BCR oligomer (Yang and Reth, 2010b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Yang and Reth, 2010b).

claim: Only a few antigen/BCR/Syk complexes can activate all antigen receptors on the B cell surface through inside-out Syk/BCR signaling, leading to signal amplification and full B cell activation.
source: With the inside-out Syk/BCR signaling process described here only a few antigen/BCR/Syk complexes can activate all antigen receptors on the B cell surface, thus leading to signal amplification and full B cell activation (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data and illustrated in Figure 5H.

claim: BCR components are frequently mutated in human leukemia.
source: Recent data show that BCR components are frequently mutated in human leukemia (Davis et al., 2010) and that an autonomously signaling BCR can act as a tumor promoter for B cell chronic lymphocytic leukemia (Duhren-von Minden et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Davis et al., 2010; Duhren-von Minden et al., 2012).

claim: An autonomously signaling BCR can act as a tumor promoter for B cell chronic lymphocytic leukemia.
source: Recent data show that BCR components are frequently mutated in human leukemia (Davis et al., 2010) and that an autonomously signaling BCR can act as a tumor promoter for B cell chronic lymphocytic leukemia (Duhren-von Minden et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Duhren-von Minden et al., 2012).

claim: TKO-MD is a pro-B cell line derived from RAG, Lambda5, SLP-65 triple-deficient mouse bone marrow which is transfected to express an IgM- and IgD-BCR specific for the hapten NIP.
source: TKO-MD is a pro-B cell line derived from RAG, Lambda5, SLP-65 triple-deficient mouse bone marrow which is transfected to express an IgM- and IgD-BCR specific for the hapten 4-hydroxy-5-iodo-3-nitrophenyl acetyl (NIP) (Meixlsperger et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Meixlsperger et al., 2007).

claim: The 2-PLA and 1-PLA are more sensitive than the Fab-PLA.
source: As indicated by the numbers of fluorescent dots, the 2-PLA and 1-PLA are more sensitive than the Fab-PLA, a phenomenon that is explained by the avidity associated with divalent antibody binding.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of fluorescent dots in the different PLA methods.

claim: The higher sensitivity of 2-PLA and 1-PLA compared to Fab-PLA is explained by the avidity associated with divalent antibody binding.
source: As indicated by the numbers of fluorescent dots, the 2-PLA and 1-PLA are more sensitive than the Fab-PLA, a phenomenon that is explained by the avidity associated with divalent antibody binding.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the understanding of antibody binding properties.

claim: Non-permeabilized, fixed B cells are used in the PLA assays to analyze the organization of molecules specifically on the cell surface without detecting intracellular complexes.
source: Importantly, we are using non-permeabilized, fixed B cells in these assays. This allows us to analyze the organization of molecules specifically on the cell surface without detecting intracellular complexes of these molecules.
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of the experimental method.

claim: PLA is a sampling method that, by measuring a few interactions per cell, allows conclusions to be drawn about the behavior of a larger pool of molecules.
source: PLA is a sampling method that, by measuring a few interactions per cell, allows conclusions to be drawn about the behavior of a larger pool of molecules.
evidence: This claim is based on the understanding of the PLA method.

claim: Increasing the Fab concentration allows measurement of many more IgM:IgM interactions on resting but not on activated B cells.
source: If we increase the Fab concentration, we can measure many more IgM:IgM interactions on resting but not on activated B cells (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1H and 1I.

claim: At high Fab concentrations, PLA signals are often overlapping, making it more difficult to quantify.
source: However, at these concentrations, the signals (red blobs) are often overlapping, making it more difficult to quantify.
evidence: This claim is based on observation of the experimental results.

claim: The loss of the PLA signal in activated B cells is not due to a loss of binding of the Fab fragment.
source: To exclude that the loss of the PLA signal in activated B cells is due to a loss of binding of the Fab fragment rather than the oligomer to monomer transition we measured the binding of all our Fab reagents by flow cytometry and found no alteration of binding between resting and activated B cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The H:L Fab-PLA signal is not altered upon B cell activation.
source: In addition we used the same anti-Ig Fabs to monitore the heavy (H) and light (L) chain interaction by H:L Fab-PLA and found, as expected, no alteration upon B cell activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The IgM:IgM and IgD:IgD Fab-PLA signal is consistently lost in activated B cells.
source: In contrast to the H:L, the IgM:IgM and IgD:IgD (see below) Fab-PLA signal is consistently lost in activated B cells suggesting that the later assays detect dynamics states of a protein complex and we think that this is the oligomer to monomer transition of the BCR.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and inference.

claim: The IgM:IgM and IgD:IgD Fab-PLA assays detect dynamic states of a protein complex, specifically the oligomer to monomer transition of the BCR.
source: In contrast to the H:L, the IgM:IgM and IgD:IgD (see below) Fab-PLA signal is consistently lost in activated B cells suggesting that the later assays detect dynamics states of a protein complex and we think that this is the oligomer to monomer transition of the BCR.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: B1-8 is a mouse whose B cells express a NIP-specific BCR.
source: We next used the Fab-PLA method to further analyze the IgM:IgM, and the IgD:IgD proximity on the surface of resting or activated spleen cells from the B1-8 mouse, whose B cells express a NIP-specific BCR (Sonoda et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Sonoda et al., 1997).

claim: Pervanadate alters the phosphorylation/dephosphorylation equilibrium.
source: The Fab-PLA signal is also lost when we stimulated B1-8 B cells apart from antigen with BCR-activating drugs such as pervanadate (Perv) and Lat-A (Figure 4C), which alter the phosphorylation/dephosphorylation equilibrium and inhibit actin polymerization, respectively (Secrist et al., 1993; Treanor et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Secrist et al., 1993; Treanor et al., 2010).

claim: Lat-A inhibits actin polymerization.
source: The Fab-PLA signal is also lost when we stimulated B1-8 B cells apart from antigen with BCR-activating drugs such as pervanadate (Perv) and Lat-A (Figure 4C), which alter the phosphorylation/dephosphorylation equilibrium and inhibit actin polymerization, respectively (Secrist et al., 1993; Treanor et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Secrist et al., 1993; Treanor et al., 2010).

claim: BCR opening does not always require the direct engagement of the receptor but can also be mediated by drugs such as Lat-A and pervanadate.
source: The above analysis shows that BCR opening does not always require the direct engagement of the receptor but can also be mediated by drugs such as Lat-A and pervanadate which alter the cytoskeleton or kinase/phosphatase equilibrium, respectively.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing BCR opening with different stimuli.

claim: Lat-A and pervanadate treatments result in strong ITAM phosphorylation.
source: These treatments also result in strong ITAM phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the effects of these drugs.

claim: The ITAM/Syk interaction is delayed but not prevented in Lyn-deficient B cells.
source: Note that the ITAM/Syk interaction is delayed but not prevented in Lyn-deficient B cells, whereas the Igα:Syk Fab-PLA in Syk-deficient B cells gave no signal due to the absence of Syk.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Lyn- and Syk-deficient B cells shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The Igα:Syk Fab-PLA in Syk-deficient B cells gave no signal due to the absence of Syk.
source: Note that the ITAM/Syk interaction is delayed but not prevented in Lyn-deficient B cells, whereas the Igα:Syk Fab-PLA in Syk-deficient B cells gave no signal due to the absence of Syk.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Syk-deficient B cells shown in Figure 5F.

claim: In the cytosol there exists an equilibrium between a closed autoinhibited and an open active form of Syk.
source: Note that in the cytosol there exists an equilibrium between a closed autoinhibited and an open active form of Syk.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Syk structure and function.

claim: The Syk inhibitor interacts only with the open active form of Syk.
source: As the inhibitor is interacting only with the latter form, it takes some time for the majority of Syk molecules in the cell to be blocked by the inhibitor.
evidence: This claim is based on understanding of how kinase inhibitors work.

claim: B cell activation involves two distinct phases: an outside-in signal and an inside-out signaling mechanism.
source: B cell activation may thus involve two distinct phases (Figure 5H). First an outside-in signal where limited amounts of antigens open a few BCR dimers, allowing them to form active BCR/Syk seed complexes that then diffuse in the membrane and phosphorylate neighboring BCR oligomers. This process then results in more Syk recruitment, BCR opening and the amplification of the BCR signal via an inside-out signaling mechanism.
evidence: This claim is a model inferred from the experimental data and illustrated in Figure 5H.

claim: Limited amounts of antigens open a few BCR dimers, allowing them to form active BCR/Syk seed complexes that diffuse in the membrane and phosphorylate neighboring BCR oligomers.
source: First an outside-in signal where limited amounts of antigens open a few BCR dimers, allowing them to form active BCR/Syk seed complexes that then diffuse in the membrane and phosphorylate neighboring BCR oligomers.
evidence: This claim is a model inferred from the experimental data.

claim: The opening of the BCR by Syk could be either due to the phosphorylation of the ITAM tyrosines or to the binding of the tandem SH2 domains to the ppITAM sequences.
source: The opening of the BCR by Syk could be either due to the phosphorylation of the ITAM tyrosines or to the binding of the tandem SH2 domains to the ppITAM sequences.
evidence: This claim presents two possible mechanisms that were tested experimentally.

claim: CD19, together with BCAP, plays an important role as an amplifier of the BCR signal in activated B cells by activating the PI-3 kinase signaling module.
source: By activating the PI-3 kinase signaling module, the CD19 coreceptor, together with the B cell adaptor for PI3K (BCAP), plays an important role as an amplifier of the BCR signal in activated B cells (Aiba et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Aiba et al., 2008).

claim: CD19-deficient B cells are defective in BCR microcluster formation.
source: CD19-deficient B cells have a compromised immune response to antigen and are defective in BCR microcluster formation (Rickert et al., 1995; Depoil et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Rickert et al., 1995; Depoil et al., 2008).

claim: BCR opening and the reorganization of co-receptors do not require the co-expression of the IgM and IgD on the cell surface.
source: BCR opening, as well as the reorganization of co-receptors, does not require the co-expression of the IgM and IgD on the cell surface.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from TKO-M and TKO-D cells shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: TKO-M and TKO-D cells that only express one class of BCR behave similarly to the TKO-MD cells.
source: TKO-M and TKO-D cells that only express one class of BCR behave similarly to the TKO-MD cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: On resting B cells, the CD19/CD20 module resides in a membrane compartment that is also targeted by the IgD-BCR but that is not dependent on IgD expression.
source: These results suggest that on resting B cells, the CD19/CD20 module resides in a membrane compartment that is also targeted by the IgD-BCR but that is not dependent on IgD expression.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing similar behavior in TKO-D cells.

claim: CTB binds with high affinity to GM1 gangliosides.
source: We labeled the cholera toxin B-subunit (CTB) with one of the PLA oligos. CTB binds with high affinity to GM1 gangliosides, glycolipids that are highly expressed in lipid ordered domains (Kenworthy et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Kenworthy et al., 2000).

claim: GM1 gangliosides are glycolipids that are highly expressed in lipid ordered domains.
source: CTB binds with high affinity to GM1 gangliosides, glycolipids that are highly expressed in lipid ordered domains (Kenworthy et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Kenworthy et al., 2000).

claim: The GPI-linked protein CD52 showed a distribution by Fab-PLA similar to that seen for the GM1 gangliosides.
source: The GPI-linked protein CD52 (Treumann et al., 1995) showed a distribution by Fab-PLA similar to that seen for the GM1 gangliosides (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 and a citation to previous work (Treumann et al., 1995).

claim: Fab-PLA allows studying the nanoscale organization of unchanged proteins on primary cells without requiring overexpression of wild type or altered (tagged) proteins in cell lines.
source: Another important advantage of Fab-PLA is that it does not require the overexpression of wild type or altered (tagged) proteins in cell lines but allows studying the nanoscale organization of unchanged proteins on primary cells.
evidence: This claim is based on the description of the Fab-PLA method.

claim: The Fab-PLA is a surprisingly robust technique that detects the same BCR alterations in B cell lines or normal B cells of either mouse or human origin, using three different stimulation protocols and different sets of Fab fragments.
source: The Fab-PLA is a surprisingly robust technique that detects the same BCR alterations in B cell lines or normal B cells of either mouse or human origin, using three different stimulation protocols and different sets of Fab fragments (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Previous live cell imaging studies of the behavior of the BCR on activated B lymphocytes have detected the formation of higher organized structures such as receptor microclusters and immunological synapses.
source: Previous live cell imaging studies of the behavior of the BCR on activated B lymphocytes have detected the formation of higher organized structures such as receptor microclusters and immunological synapses (Treanor and Batista, 2007; Tolar et al., 2008; Harwood and Batista, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Treanor and Batista, 2007; Tolar et al., 2008; Harwood and Batista, 2011).

claim: Previous live cell imaging studies have suggested that receptor aggregation rather than dissociation is the earliest event in B cell activation.
source: These studies have suggested that receptor aggregation rather than dissociation is the earliest event in B cell activation.
evidence: This claim is based on interpretation of previous live cell imaging studies.

claim: Due to the diffraction barrier of visible light of 250 nm, live cell imaging studies could never directly monitor the conformation and nanoscale organization of the BCR on resting or activated B cells.
source: However, due to the diffraction barrier of visible light of 250 nm (Huang et al., 2010), these live cell imaging studies could never directly monitor the conformation and nanoscale organization of the BCR on resting or activated B cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Huang et al., 2010) and established knowledge about the diffraction limit.

claim: The existence of antigen receptor nanoclusters or protein islands was first indicated by electron microscopy studies.
source: The existence of these structures was first indicated by electron microscopy studies (Wilson et al., 2000) and recently confirmed by photo-activated localization microscopy (PALM) (Lillemeier et al., 2006, 2010; Sherman et al., 2011) and direct stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (dSTORM) (Mattila et al., 2013; Owen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Wilson et al., 2000; Lillemeier et al., 2006, 2010; Sherman et al., 2011; Mattila et al., 2013; Owen et al., 2013).

claim: The existence of antigen receptor nanoclusters or protein islands was recently confirmed by PALM and dSTORM.
source: The existence of these structures was first indicated by electron microscopy studies (Wilson et al., 2000) and recently confirmed by photo-activated localization microscopy (PALM) (Lillemeier et al., 2006, 2010; Sherman et al., 2011) and direct stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (dSTORM) (Mattila et al., 2013; Owen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Lillemeier et al., 2006, 2010; Sherman et al., 2011; Mattila et al., 2013; Owen et al., 2013).

claim: The TCR exists in an equilibrium between monomeric and oligomeric forms.
source: In contrast to the BCR which is predominantly oligomeric, the T cell antigen receptor (TCR) seems to exist in an equilibrium between monomeric and oligomeric forms (Schamel et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Schamel et al., 2005).

claim: TCR nanoclusters are more variable in size than the BCR nanoclusters.
source: This may be the reason why TCR nanoclusters are more variable in size than the BCR nanoclusters (Lillemeier et al., 2010; Sherman et al., 2011; Mattila et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Lillemeier et al., 2010; Sherman et al., 2011; Mattila et al., 2013) and inference.

claim: Upon activation, nanoclusters can form microclusters or cap structures.
source: However, common to the two cell types is the finding that upon activation the nanoclusters can form microclusters or cap structures (Lillemeier et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Lillemeier et al., 2010).

claim: Fab-PLA makes it possible to explore the organization of receptors on the surface of normal B cells in the 10-20 nm range.
source: The Fab-PLA method we have developed, makes it possible, for the first time, to explore the organization of receptors on the surface of normal B cells in the 10–20 nm range.
evidence: This claim is supported by the description and validation of the Fab-PLA method in the manuscript.

claim: The reason why only Fab-PLA can reliably monitor the alterations of the BCR conformation may be related to the structure of this receptor.
source: The reason why only Fab-PLA can reliably monitor the alterations of the BCR conformation may be related to the structure of this receptor.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference about the BCR structure.

claim: The BCR contains flexible Fab arms and it may be the extension of these arms that moves the BCR monomers apart from each other so that Fab-PLA can no longer detect their proximity.
source: Like an antibody, the BCR contains flexible Fab arms and it maybe the extension of these arms that moves the BCR monomers apart from each other so that Fab-PLA can no longer detect their proximity (Figure 1J).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference about the BCR structure and illustrated in Figure 1J.
